script.title: Why Hooke Melted Glass Into Tiny Beads

lines: A scientist melted the end of a glass thread into a tiny bead.
His name was Robert Hooke, and in his youth he was poor.
Back then, the microscope was still largely a novelty.
Hooke wanted to study living things at a tiny scale.
So he fused the ends of spun glass threads into small glass balls.
Each little ball became a lens.
Hooke designed his own microscope too.
Christopher Cock made it for him in London, in leather and gold.
You see, it's like a water drop on a leaf, making the veins under it look bigger.
In 1663 and 1664, Hooke peered into a hidden world.
He made the earliest recorded sighting of a microorganism, a tiny mould called Mucor.
Plant structures looked like the cells of a honeycomb.
In 1665, his book Micrographia came out.
Its impressive pictures gave it a huge impact.
Samuel Pepys sat up until two o'clock reading it.
Then, after the Great Fire of London in 1666, Hooke surveyed more than half the property lines.
The man who studied tiny cells helped rebuild a whole city.

claims.claim: Hooke created tiny lenses of small glass globules made by fusing the ends of threads of spun glass.
Hooke was an impoverished scientific inquirer in young adulthood.
The microscope was still largely a novelty until the 1660s and 1670s, when naturalists in Italy, the Netherlands and England began using them to study biology.
Hooke was one of the first scientists to investigate living things at microscopic scale, using a compound microscope that he designed.
The hand-crafted, leather-and-gold-tooled microscope Hooke designed was made for him in London by Christopher Cock.
In 1663 and 1664 Hooke made his microscopic observations; Micrographia contains the earliest-recorded observation of a microorganism, the microfungus Mucor.
Hooke coined the term cell, suggesting a resemblance between plant structures and honeycomb cells.
Micrographia was published in 1665 and had a huge impact, largely because of its impressive illustrations.
Samuel Pepys wrote in his diary that he sat up till two o'clock in his chamber reading Hooke's book.
After the Great Fire of London in 1666, Hooke performed more than half of the property line surveys and assisted with the city's rapid reconstruction.

cast.pepys: a 31 year old English gentleman, plump round face, a long dark brown curled wig, a thin dark moustache, wearing a deep green velvet coat with white lace cuffs, 1660s
